A **breadboard** lets you build circuits without soldering. Under the holes, metal spring clips grip the legs of your parts and connect them.

The holes are connected in groups:

- In the middle, each **row** of 5 holes is one connected strip. On most boards the columns are lettered a to e and f to j, and the rows are numbered. Holes 12a, 12b, 12c, 12d and 12e are all connected.
- A **gap** runs down the centre. In row 12, holes a to e are **not** connected to holes f to j. A chip sits across the gap, so each of its legs gets its own strip.
- Along the long edges run the **power rails**, marked + (often red) and − (often blue). Each rail is connected along its length.

Two parts are connected when they share a strip. To connect parts in series, the two legs of each part go in different rows, and the next part starts in the row where the last one ended.

Classic mistakes:

- Both legs of one part in the same row. The strip joins the legs, so the current goes around the part instead of through it.
- On some long boards the power rails are split in the middle. Look for a break in the red and blue lines, or check with a multimeter.
- The rails on the two sides of the board are not joined to each other. Add wires if you use both.
lessons.task: You push a red LED into a breadboard with its long leg in hole 12a and its short leg in hole 12c. The rest of the circuit is fine. What happens?
lessons.hint: Which holes on a breadboard are connected to each other?

options: It stays dark, because the row's strip joins its two legs together
It lights normally, because each leg is in its own hole
It lights dimly, because the strip adds some resistance
It burns out, because the strip puts the full battery voltage across it
why: Right. Holes 12a and 12c are on the same strip, so the current takes the easy path through the metal clip and none goes through the LED.
Each leg has its own hole, but both holes are in row 12, which is one connected strip. What matters is the strip, not the hole.
The clips are metal with almost no resistance. The LED is bypassed, not dimmed.
The strip joins the two legs, so there is almost 0 V between them. With no voltage across it, no current flows through the LED.
check.explain: Holes a to e in one row share one metal strip. With both legs in row 12, the LED's legs are joined together, so the current flows through the strip and bypasses the LED. Move one leg to another row.

lessons.title: The Multimeter
lessons.goal: Measure voltage, current and resistance with a multimeter the right way.
lessons.theory:
A **multimeter** measures voltage, current and resistance. It has a dial, two probes (black and red) and a few sockets.

- **Black probe:** always in the socket marked **COM**.
- **Red probe:** in the socket marked **VΩ** for voltage and resistance, and in the socket marked **mA** (or **10A** for big currents) for current.

**Voltage** (DC volts, marked V with a solid and a dashed line): voltage is measured **across** a part. With the circuit on, touch the probes to both ends of the part, so the meter sits **in parallel** with it.

**Current** (A or mA): the current must flow **through** the meter. Switch off, break the loop at one point and put the meter in the gap, so it is **in series**. Then switch on and read. In current mode the meter is almost a plain wire. Never put it across a battery or a part in this mode: that makes a short circuit and blows the meter's fuse, or worse.

**Resistance** (Ω): the meter sends its own tiny current, so the **power must be off**. Take the part out if you can, because other parts connected to it change the reading.

**Continuity** (the beep): the meter beeps when two points are connected. Use it, power off, to check wires and rows.

After measuring current, move the red probe back to the VΩ socket. Forgetting this blows fuses.

Your multimeter is for low-voltage projects only. Never measure a wall socket or anything plugged into the mains.
lessons.task: You want to measure how much current flows in your LED circuit. How do you connect the multimeter?
lessons.hint: Voltage is measured across a part; current is measured through it. Which option makes the current flow through the meter?

options: With the circuit on, touch the probes across the LED, dial on DC volts
With the circuit on, touch the probes across the battery, dial on mA
With the circuit off, touch the probes across the LED, dial on Ω
Break the loop and put the meter in the gap, red probe in mA, dial on mA
why: That measures the voltage across the LED, not the current. Current has to flow through the meter.
In current mode the meter is almost a plain wire. Across the battery it makes a short circuit and blows the fuse.
That measures resistance, not current. With the power off, no current flows at all.
Right. The current has to flow through the meter, so the meter must become part of the loop, in series.
check.explain: To measure current, the current has to flow through the meter. Break the loop, put the meter in the gap in series with the red probe in the mA socket and the dial on mA, then switch on and read.

lessons.title: Reading a Schematic
lessons.goal: Recognise the basic schematic symbols, and read which way an LED points.
lessons.theory:
A **schematic** is a map of a circuit. It shows what is connected to what, not where the parts sit on the board. Lines are wires.

The symbols you will meet most:

- **Battery:** a long line and a short line side by side. The long line is **+**, the short line is **−**. Several pairs mean several cells.
- **Resistor:** a zigzag line, or a small rectangle in European drawings. Its value is written beside it, such as 330 Ω.
- **Diode:** a triangle pointing at a bar. Current flows the way the triangle points: into the wide end, the **anode**, and out through the bar, the **cathode**.
- **LED:** a diode symbol with two small arrows pointing away from it, for the light it gives out.
- **Switch:** a line with a gap and a short lever tilted up, drawn open.
- **Ground:** three horizontal lines getting shorter, like an upside-down triangle. It is the 0 V point. All ground symbols in a drawing are connected, even without a line between them.

Two more rules:

- A **dot** where wires meet means they are connected. Wires that cross **without** a dot are not connected.
- On a real LED the anode is the long leg; the cathode is the short leg, next to a flat edge on the LED's rim.

A simple LED circuit, following the loop:

```text
battery + → switch → 330 Ω resistor → LED (anode → cathode) → battery −
```
lessons.task: In a schematic, an LED's triangle points to the right, at a bar. Which way does current flow through it, and which leg of the real LED is the bar?
lessons.hint: Think of the triangle as an arrow. What is the bar called, and which leg is that?

options: Left to right; the bar is the cathode, the short leg
Right to left; the bar is the anode, the long leg
Left to right; the bar is the anode, the long leg
Either way; the symbol only shows where the LED sits
why: Right. Current flows the way the triangle points, into the bar. The bar is the cathode: the short leg next to the flat edge.
The triangle is an arrow for current, and here it points left to right. The bar marks the cathode, not the anode.
The direction is right, but the bar is the cathode (short leg). The anode is at the wide end of the triangle.
An LED is a diode, so current flows one way only, the way the triangle points. And a schematic shows connections, not where parts sit.
check.explain: The triangle points the way current flows, from anode to cathode. The bar is the cathode, which is the LED's short leg next to the flat edge of its rim.

lessons.title: Battery Safety
lessons.goal: See why a short circuit is dangerous, and handle batteries safely.
lessons.theory:
Batteries store a lot of energy and can release it fast. Common types:

- **Alkaline** cells, such as the AA (1.5 V) and the 9 V block.
- **Lithium** cells, lithium-ion and LiPo: about **3.7 V** each, and 4.2 V when full. They store a lot of energy for their weight.

A **short circuit** is a path from + to − with almost no resistance: a loose wire, a metal tool, or coins and keys in a pocket touching both ends. The only resistance left is the wire and the battery's own small **internal resistance**, so by Ohm's law:

```text
short-circuit current = battery voltage / (internal resistance + wire resistance)
```

Example: a 1.5 V AA cell with 0.2 Ω in total gives 1.5 / 0.2 = 7.5 A. That current turns into heat. Lithium cells have a much lower internal resistance, so the current is far bigger. They can swell, burst or catch fire, and a lithium fire is very hard to put out.

Rules that keep you safe:

- Never short a battery. Carry loose cells in a case, never loose in a pocket.
- Check the **polarity** (+ and −) before you connect. Backwards, parts can die at once.
- Never use a battery that is swollen, dented, leaking or hot. Stop, keep it away from anything that can burn, and tell an adult.
- Charge lithium cells only with the right charger, on a surface that cannot burn, and never leave them charging unattended.
lessons.task: A 3.7 V lithium cell is shorted by a piece of wire. The cell's internal resistance and the wire add up to 0.05 Ω. What current flows? Answer in A, rounded to a whole number.
lessons.hint: Use Ohm's law with the total resistance of the loop: current equals voltage divided by resistance.

check.explain: Current = 3.7 V / 0.05 Ω = **74 A**. That is thousands of times what an LED needs, and it makes about 3.7 V × 74 A ≈ 274 W of heat (P = V × I) in a thin wire and a small cell. That is why a short circuit can start a fire.

lessons.title: Soldering and Workshop Safety
lessons.goal: Learn the safety rules for soldering and for working at the bench.
lessons.theory:
**Soldering** joins parts for good with melted metal called solder. The tip of a soldering iron runs at about **350 °C**, hot enough to burn skin instantly and to melt plastic.

The iron:

- Always put it back in its **stand**, even for a few seconds. Never lay it on the bench.
- Hold it by the grip, like a pen. Treat the metal as hot even after switching off: it takes minutes to cool.
- If it falls, **let it fall**. Step back and never try to catch it. Pick it up by the grip once it has landed.
- Keep its cable, and all other cables, away from the hot tip.
- Unplug it when you are done.

Fumes and solder:

- The smoke comes from the flux inside the solder. Work with good ventilation or a fume extractor, and keep your face out of the smoke.
- Some solder contains lead, so lead-free solder is better. Either way, do not eat at the bench, and wash your hands afterwards.

Eyes:

- Wear **safety glasses**. Solder can spit, and the legs you clip off can fly into an eye. Hold a leg while you clip it.

Working on circuits:

- Switch the power off before you change anything.
- Only work on low-voltage circuits. Mains electricity from wall sockets can kill: never open anything that plugs into the wall.

If you burn yourself, cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, and tell an adult.
lessons.task: Your friend knocks a hot soldering iron off its stand, and it starts to fall off the bench. What should you do?
lessons.hint: Think about which part of the iron your hand might grab while it is falling.

options: Catch it quickly, before it damages the floor
Let it fall, then pick it up by the grip
Catch it with a cloth so your hand is protected
Pull it back up by its cable before it lands
why: You might grab the 350 °C metal. A scorched floor is far better than a burnt hand.
Right. A falling iron is too hot and too fast to catch safely. Let it land, then pick it up by the grip.
A cloth does not protect you from 350 °C metal for long, and it could scorch or catch fire.
The iron swings on its cable, and the hot tip could hit you, the bench or the cable itself.
check.explain: Never try to catch a falling soldering iron. Step back, let it land, and pick it up by the grip. Then check its cable for damage before you use it again.

lessons.title: Challenge: The LED That Won't Light
lessons.goal: Use your multimeter and a clear method to find out why an LED circuit does not work.
lessons.theory:
When a circuit does not work, do not pull it apart. Measure it.

A useful fact: in a series loop, **if no current flows, a resistor has 0 V across it**, because V = I × R and I is 0. The whole supply voltage then appears across the **gap**: the one place that blocks the current. So with the meter on DC volts, look for the part with the full battery voltage across it. That is where the loop is broken.

For comparison, a working red LED circuit on 9 V has about 2 V across the LED and about 7 V across the resistor.

A method, in order:

- **Power:** measure the battery. A flat battery shows much less than its label says.
- **Voltages:** measure across each part and compare with the working circuit above.
- **Polarity:** is the LED's long leg (anode) towards +? An LED in backwards blocks all current.
- **Breadboard:** are both legs of a part in one row? Is a rail split? Is a wire one row off?
- **Values:** is the resistor the one you meant? 470 kΩ instead of 470 Ω lets through a thousand times less current, so the LED stays dark or barely glimmers. Most of the voltage then sits across the resistor.
- **Continuity:** with the power off, use the beep to check wires and rows.

Change one thing at a time, then measure again.

For this final challenge, trust the numbers, not a guess.
lessons.task: Your circuit is a 9 V battery, a 470 Ω resistor and a red LED in one series loop on a breadboard. The LED is new and you tested it this morning, but now it stays dark. With the meter on DC volts you measure **9 V** across the battery, **0 V** across the resistor and **9 V** across the LED. What is the most likely cause?
lessons.hint: 0 V across the resistor tells you how much current flows. Then find the part with the full 9 V across it.

options: The battery is flat and gives no current
A wire is one row off, leaving a gap in the loop
The LED is in backwards, so it blocks the current
The resistor is 470 kΩ instead of 470 Ω
why: The battery shows its full 9 V, so it is fine.
That gap would block the current too, but then the 9 V would appear across the gap and the LED would show 0 V. Your meter shows 9 V across the LED, so the LED itself is the gap.

Right. 0 V across the resistor means no current flows, and the full 9 V across the LED means the LED is what blocks the loop. A new LED you tested this morning is almost certainly in backwards. Turn it round.
A 470 kΩ resistor still lets a tiny current through, so most of the 9 V would sit across the resistor, not 0 V.
check.explain: 0 V across the resistor means no current flows (V = I × R). The full 9 V sits across the LED, so the LED is the part blocking the loop. Since you know it works, it is in backwards: turn it so its long leg faces +.
